title: Maritime Psychology: Definition, Scope and Conceptualization
central_proposition: This chapter defines maritime psychology as the study and practice of the interplay between human behavior and the maritime environment, advocating for a systems perspective to integrate psychological research across individual, team, organizational, business, and industry levels within the maritime transport sector to enhance safety, health, and performance.

concept_definitions.name: Maritime psychology
concept_definitions.definition: the study and practice of the interplay between human behaviour and the maritime environment.

concept_definitions.name: Human element
concept_definitions.definition: the “marinized” term used to describe at least some of the aspects of psychology in the maritime field.

concept_definitions.name: Psychological capital (PsyCap)
concept_definitions.definition: combines four somewhat related “good things”, these being Hope, Resiliency, Optimism and Self-Efficacy.

argument_structure: The chapter establishes maritime psychology as a distinct field, defines its scope through a classification of maritime activities, and argues for a systems-based approach to understanding human factors in the maritime transport industry. It presents a nested model illustrating the interconnectedness of individual, team, organizational, business, and industry levels, and discusses various challenges and opportunities for psychological research and intervention within this framework.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Human behavior and well-being in the maritime environment are shaped by a complex interplay of factors across multiple nested systemic levels (individual, team, organization, business, industry). Interventions must therefore adopt a holistic, systems perspective to be effective, as isolated individual-level approaches may be counterproductive or misattribute systemic issues to individuals. Psychosocial factors, if not adequately addressed, can lead to negative outcomes in safety, health, and performance. Conversely, positive psychological approaches and human-centered design can foster well-being and improve outcomes.

findings.antecedent: Psychosocial factors (e.g., work roles, manning, piracy, trauma, crisis, environmental health challenges, dangerous cargoes, motion sickness, shipwreck, fatigue, working conditions, leisure time, privacy, social opportunities)
findings.mechanism: These factors directly influence the psychological state and physical health of seafarers, impacting their ability to perform tasks safely and efficiently.
findings.quote: It covers a range of issues where psychological factors are of clear importance.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Carter and Schreiner (2013) 'Textbook of Maritime Medicine' outlines these issues.

findings.antecedent: Systems perspective (integrating individual, team, organizational, business, and industry levels)
findings.consequent: Effectiveness of psychological interventions in maritime transport
findings.mechanism: A holistic understanding of the nested system allows for targeted and effective interventions, preventing misattribution of systemic failings to individuals and ensuring comprehensive change.
findings.source: Page 14, Introduction & Page 21, text below Figure 1
findings.quote: its application in the maritime transport sector requires a systems perspective

findings.antecedent: Maritime environment (as a beneficial intervention, e.g., sailing)
findings.mechanism: The unique context of the maritime environment can provide opportunities for personal growth, healing, calmness, invigoration, education, and self-development.
findings.quote: the psychological benefit of the maritime as a beneficial intervention.

findings.antecedent: Ship design (e.g., living space, communal areas)
findings.mechanism: Physical structure directly influences social structure and psychological experience, affecting sleep quality, fatigue, privacy, attitudes to safety, and crew retention.
findings.quote: the design of living space on board will reflect the legislative environment and the attitude of the company towards social spaces

findings.mechanism: Democratic command styles and a culture that cultivates diversity of views foster a better working environment and improved problem-solving, contributing to better safety.
findings.quote: certain styles of command—generally more democratic styles—are associated with better sea farer well-being.
findings.empirical_support_cited: O’Shea (2005), MacLachlan and O’Connell (2000), Cox and Blake (1991)

findings.consequent: Perceptions of safety climate, job satisfaction, organizational effectiveness, positive work outcomes
findings.mechanism: PsyCap, comprising hope, resiliency, optimism, and self-efficacy, is a motivational state that positively influences how individuals perceive safety and their overall work experience.
findings.quote: This motivational state has been shown to be related to organizational effectiveness and positive work outcomes
findings.empirical_support_cited: Newman et al. (2014), Bergheim et al. (2015)

findings.consequent: Generalizability of PsyCap benefits, effectiveness of interventions
findings.mechanism: Cultural context influences how PsyCap is associated with outcomes and how interventions are received, meaning what works for one dominant group may not work for others.
findings.quote: this indirect effect was evidenced only for European and not for Filipino crew. So while PsyCap may be associated with benefits for some groups, its potential for promoting comprehensive change for all members of a ship’s crew has yet to be demonstrated
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bergheim et al. (2015), MacLachlan and O’Connell (2000)

findings.antecedent: Stigma (regarding mental health problems among seafarers)
findings.mechanism: Fear of losing jobs or not being rehired due to mental health issues discourages seafarers from seeking necessary support, highlighting the interaction between individual and systemic factors.
findings.quote: Stigma discourages many seafarers from seeking consultation or effective therapy … because they fear losing their jobs or not being rehired

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Positive psychology interventions and training enhance well-being, performance, and safety in the maritime workplace, and the mechanisms of these interventions are transferable to the maritime environment.
Specific facilitators and barriers exist for the effective implementation of positive psychology interventions in the maritime context.
Positive psychology interventions show signs of effect maintenance in the maritime context over time.
Positive psychology interventions offer advantages or disadvantages relative to other forms of psychological intervention in the maritime context.
Positive psychology computer-based interventions and training are an effective and viable option in the maritime context.
A systems-based approach to research and implementation can facilitate integrated health care interventions in the maritime environment.
bridge_warrants: The chapter connects maritime psychology to global health, occupational health, and organizational psychology.
It draws on the 'human element' concept from maritime regulation as a 'marinized' term for psychology.
It utilizes a systems perspective, drawing on previous work (MacLachlan et al. 2013) and the STAMINA model of human factors (Koumaditis et al. 2011) from aviation.
It highlights the interplay between social, biological, physical, and environmental perspectives in understanding maritime psychology.
methodological_critiques: The scope of psychology in the commercial transport sector remains quite underdeveloped.
Existing models for ship evacuation may not adequately consider the frailty, mobility, cognitive, or sensory impairments of passengers.
PsyCap benefits may not generalize to all crew members, especially across different cultures, requiring careful exploration.

Research designs in maritime health need to be more ambitious and robust, including randomized controlled trials, longitudinal studies, qualitative research, and focus on non-European seafarers, spouses, and family members.
model_structure: The chapter proposes a 'nested model of the psychosocial and organisational aspects of maritime work' (Figure 1, Page 21). This model consists of five concentric levels: Job, Person (Individual), Ship (Team), Company (Business), and Industry. Each level represents different factors influencing maritime work, and these levels are conceptualized as continually interacting, implying that interventions at one level can affect others.
limitations: The volume is not exhaustive or comprehensive in its coverage of maritime psychology.
The definition of maritime psychology is presented as evolving and potentially contested.
The primary focus of the book is on commercial maritime transport, not encompassing all aspects of maritime psychology (e.g., leisure, military).
The military aspects of the maritime, while acknowledged as important, are not covered in this volume.
The maritime environment is vast, and people perceive opportunities and threats differently within it.

paper_metadata.title: Patterns of Growth—Biomimetics and Architectural Design
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Patterns of Growth—Biomimetics and Architectural Design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper discusses the approach of biomimetic design in architecture applied to the theme of growth in biology by taking two exemplary research projects at the intersection of arts and sciences. The first project, ‘Biornametics’, dealt with patterns from nature; the second project ‘Growing as Building (GrAB)’ took on biological growth as a specific theme for the transfer to architecture and the arts. Within a timeframe of five years (2011–2015), the research was conducted under the Program for Arts-based Research PEEK (Programm zur Entwicklung und Erschliessung der Künste) of the Austrian Science Fund FWF (Fonds zur Förderung der wissenschaftlichen Forschung). The underlying hypothesis was that growth processes in nature have not been studied for transfer into technology and architecture yet and that, with advanced software tools, promising applications could be found. To ensure a high degree of innovation, this research was done with an interdisciplinary team of architects, engineers, and scientists (mainly biologists) to lay the groundwork for future product-oriented technological solutions. Growth, as one of the important characteristics of living organisms, is used as a frame for research into systems and principles that shall deliver innovative and sustainable solutions in architecture and the arts. Biomimetics as a methodology was used to create and guide information transfer from the life sciences to innovative proto-architectural solutions. The research aimed at transferring qualities present in biological growth; for example, adaptiveness, exploration, or local resource harvesting into technical design and production processes. In contrast to our current building construction, implementing principles of growth could potentially transform building towards a more integrated and sustainable setting, a new living architecture. Tools and methods, especially Quality Function Deployment (QFD) for matching biological role models with growth principles and architecturally desired functions and a Biolab as an experimentation platform are presented. Three main experimental trajectories were explored that matched the objectives of the research: (1) Transfer from biology into architecture, namely self-growing structures (proto-steps in form of a mobile 3D printer working with local material); (2) Integration of biology into material systems, namely fragmented waste matter grown into one solid building material (mycelium); and (3) Interventions in existing architecture, namely optimization of 3D path-finding through a single cell organism (slime mold).

theory_commitments.specific_claim: This paper proposes a comprehensive conceptual framework defining maritime psychology, outlining its scope, and identifying key psychosocial and environmental factors influencing seafarer health, well-being, and performance.
